chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Majiluwayh narrated to me from his uncle Muhammad ibn Abi al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Husayn ibn Ali from Ishaq ibn Ammar from Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

One who recites a hundred verses, praying with them in one night, Allah will record for him the reward of standing in prayer for that night; and one who recites two hundred verses in a night apart from the Night Prayer, Allah will write for him in the Tablet a Qintar of good deeds. And a Qintar is a thousand and two hundred Awqiya, and an Awqiya is greater than Mount Uhud.

key_terms.أُوقِیَّهٍ: An Awqiya, a unit of weight used to measure the Qintar
key_terms.جَبَلِ أُحُدٍ: Mount Uhud, used here as a metaphor for immense size
key_terms.صَلَاهِ اللَّیْلِ: Night Prayer (specifically Tarawih or Tahajjud context)
key_terms.قُنُوتَ لَیْلَهٍ: Standing in prayer for the whole night (reward)
key_terms.قِنْطَاراً: A Qintar, a large unit of weight or measure for good deeds

ai.seo_question: What is the reward for reciting 100 or 200 verses of the Quran at night?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights the immense spiritual economy of Quranic recitation, equating the brevity of reciting one hundred verses with the prolonged devotion of a full night's prayer (Qunut al-Layl). The mention of the 'Qintar'—a weight of good deeds exceeding Mount Uhud—serves as a vivid metaphor for the exponential reward of consistent, even brief, engagement with the Divine Word outside formal ritual.

en.sayed-athar-husain-rizvi-&-sayed-maqs: 1. It was narrated to me by Muhammad b. Ali b. Majluwayh from his uncle Muhammad b. Abi al-Qasim from Muhammad b. Isa from al-Hussain b. Ali from Ishaq b. Ammar from Abi Abdillah (a.s.) who said: “

One who recites a hundred verses in Salaat-e-Shab, Allah would note down the reward of offering Salaat for the whole night for him and one who recites two hundred verses at night apart from Salaat-e-Shab, the Almighty Allah would write a Qintar of good deeds on Lauh-e-Mahfuz. A single Qintar is equal to twelve hundred Awqiya and a single Awqiya is bigger that Mount Ohad.”
